title: Branches, Procedures and Translating High-Level Code
subtitle: How if, loops, arrays and function calls become assembly.

references.title: Instructions: Language of the Computer
references.topics: Instructions for making decisions; supporting procedures in computer hardware (the stack, $ra, spilling); translating loops and arrays

objectives: Translate if and if-else statements into MIPS using branch instructions
Translate while and for loops and an array traversal
Use jump instructions: j, jal and jr
Explain how a procedure call and return use $ra
Use the stack to save registers and explain register spilling

steps.question: A processor can only add, load, store and compare. So how does it run `if`, `while` and function calls?
clues: An `if` becomes a **branch** that skips instructions.
A loop is a branch that jumps **backwards**.
A function call is a **jump that remembers where to come back**.

notes.explain: Let students guess before revealing the clues.
Read the objectives aloud; they return in the learning report.

steps.title: Branch and jump instructions

head: Instruction
What it does
Type
rows: Go to label if rs equals rt
Go to label if rs differs from rt
Go to label and save the return address in $ra
Go to the address held in rs

steps.why: Conditional branches only test equality. Anything else (less than, greater than) is built from `slt` plus a branch.
steps.real: Every `if`, loop condition and function call in a program becomes one of these six instructions.

mistake.wrong: MIPS has a single instruction that branches when a < b.
mistake.right: Compare with slt first, then branch on the 0 or 1 result with beq or bne.

explainAgain.beginner: Equality is cheap to test in hardware; less-than needs a subtraction. MIPS keeps the branch simple and uses slt for the comparison.

steps.title: Translating if-else
steps.why: The branch tests the opposite of the condition: when a < b is false, skip over the then-part.

deeper.text: The `j done` after the then-part is essential. Without it the else-part runs too.

steps.title: Predict, then run

blocks.title: if (a < b) x = y; else x = z;
blocks.program:
slt $t0, $s0, $s1
beq $t0, $zero, else
add $s2, $zero, $s3
j done
else: add $s2, $zero, $s4
done:
blocks.hint: a = 3 and b = 7. Change $s0 to 9 and $s1 to 2 and run again.

steps.why: The same program takes a different path for different data.

steps.question: With a = 3 and b = 7, what is `$s2` when the program finishes?

reveal.text: 3 < 7, so `slt` sets $t0 = 1, the `beq` is not taken and `add $s2, $zero, $s3` runs, giving **111**. Then `j done` skips the else-part.

steps.result: Check what happens with a = 9 and b = 2: $t0 = 0, the branch is taken and x = 222.

steps.title: If without else
steps.why: Again the branch tests the opposite condition: not equal means skip the increment.
steps.real: Checking an error code or a missing value before acting on it uses this exact shape.

steps.title: Run the if without else

blocks.title: if (a == b) c = c + 1;
blocks.hint: Equal values give $s2 = 11. Change $s1 to 5 and $s2 stays 10.

steps.why: Try both outcomes before moving on.

steps.question: Which instruction pair tests `a < b` and jumps to `L` when it is true?
steps.why: slt makes $t0 = 1 exactly when a < b, and bne to $zero branches when $t0 is not 0.
feedback: The comparison must be against $zero, because $t0 is a 0 or 1 flag.
j always jumps, with no test.

steps.title: Find the mistake
steps.prompt: This if-else translation has a bug. Click the faulty line.
steps.explain: The then-part needs a `j done` before `else`, otherwise the else-part also runs and overwrites x.

steps.title: A loop is a backward branch

head: Java / C
MIPS idea
rows: Test at the top; exit when the test fails
`j loop` jumps back to the test

nodes.label: Test
nodes.note: Leave the loop when the condition is false.

steps.why: All loops (while, for, do-while) are conditional branches plus a backward jump.
steps.real: A for loop over millions of items is the same few instructions repeated.

explainAgain.beginner: Picture a race track: the jump at the end sends you back to the start line, and the test is the gate that lets you off the track.

steps.title: while: doubling five times

steps.note: The test: slt/slti plus beq to leave the loop.
The body: sll by 1 doubles $t1; addi adds 1 to $t0.
j loop: jump back to the test.

blocks.title: while (i < 5) { t = t * 2; i++; }
blocks.program:
addi $t0, $zero, 0
addi $t1, $zero, 1
loop: slti $t2, $t0, 5
beq $t2, $zero, end
sll $t1, $t1, 1
addi $t0, $t0, 1
j loop
end:
blocks.hint: Step through and watch $t1 double each time. Predict the final $t1.

steps.why: Shifting left by 1 multiplies by 2, so five iterations give 2^5 = 32.

steps.question: What are `$t0` and `$t1` when the while loop ends?

reveal.text: The loop runs for i = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4: five iterations. $t0 = 5, and $t1 = 1 × 2⁵ = **32**.

steps.result: The test fails when i reaches 5, so the body never runs a sixth time.

steps.title: for: summing 0 to 5
steps.why: A for loop is a while loop with the initialization and update written in one place.

steps.title: Run the for loop

blocks.title: for (i = 0; i < 6; i++) sum += i;
blocks.program:
addi $t0, $zero, 0
addi $t1, $zero, 0
for: slti $t2, $t0, 6
beq $t2, $zero, end
add $t1, $t1, $t0
addi $t0, $t0, 1
j for
end:

steps.why: Check that the sum is 15 and that i ends at 6, not 5.

steps.title: Arrays: index to address
steps.why: Memory is addressed in bytes, so element i of an int array lives 4 × i bytes after the start.
steps.real: Every a[i] in Java, C or Python is compiled to this multiply-and-add.

mistake.wrong: Element i is at base + i.
mistake.right: Elements are 4 bytes wide, so the offset is 4 × i.

explainAgain.beginner: A row of mailboxes numbered 0, 4, 8, 12... Mailbox i has number 4i.

steps.title: Array traversal

blocks.title: Sum the array a[0..4]
blocks.program:
addi $t0, $zero, 0
lui $s0, 0x1001
add $t3, $zero, $zero
loop: slti $t1, $t0, 5
beq $t1, $zero, end
sll $t2, $t0, 2
add $t2, $t2, $s0
lw $t4, 0($t2)
add $t3, $t3, $t4
addi $t0, $t0, 1
j loop
end:
blocks.hint: The array starts at 0x10010000. $t3 collects the sum.

steps.why: $s0 holds the base address; each pass computes the element address, loads it and adds it.

steps.question: What is `$t3` after the array traversal?
steps.result: Add the five elements. 45 would be the sum of the first four only.

steps.title: Mini challenge
steps.prompt: Put the body of the array-sum loop in order.
items: Test i < 5 and leave if false
Add it to the sum, then i = i + 1 and jump back
steps.why: The address must be built before it can be used to load.

steps.statement: A `for` loop needs a different set of hardware instructions than a `while` loop.
steps.why: Both are built from the same compare, branch and jump instructions.

questions.q: Why does a loop end with a backward jump?
questions.a: So that execution returns to the test and repeats.

questions.q: How do you compute the address of a[i] for an int array?
How do you branch when a < b?
questions.a: slt to make a 0/1 flag, then bne or beq against $zero.

steps.title: Calling and returning

nodes.label: Caller sets arguments
nodes.note: Put values in the argument registers.

nodes.label: jal
nodes.note: Saves PC + 4 in $ra, then jumps to the procedure.

nodes.label: Procedure runs
nodes.note: Does the work and puts the result in $v0 and $v1.

nodes.label: jr $ra
nodes.note: Jumps back to the instruction after the jal.

head: Register
Role
rows: must be preserved by the callee

steps.why: `jal` and `jr $ra` let any code call a procedure from anywhere and come back to the right place.
steps.real: This is every function and method call in Java, C or Python.

mistake.wrong: jr $ra is a special return instruction.
mistake.right: It is a normal jump to a register; $ra just happens to hold the return address.

explainAgain.beginner: Like a bookmark: jal puts a bookmark in $ra, and jr $ra goes back to it.

steps.title: A leaf procedure

blocks.title: jal and jr $ra
blocks.program:
addi $a0, $zero, 6
addi $a1, $zero, 7
jal addtwice
addi $s0, $v0, 0
j end
addtwice: add $t0, $a0, $a1
sll $v0, $t0, 1
jr $ra
end:
blocks.hint: Watch $ra after jal. It holds the address of the instruction after the call.

steps.why: A procedure that calls no other procedure needs no stack: this is a leaf.

steps.question: After `jal addtwice` at address 0x00400008, what is `$ra`?

reveal.text: jal saves **PC + 4**, the address of the next instruction: 0x00400008 + 4 = **0x0040000C**.

steps.result: The return address is the instruction after the call, not the call itself.

steps.question: What does `jr $ra` do?
options: Jumps to the address stored in $ra
Jumps to the label named ra
steps.why: It loads the PC from $ra, returning to the caller.
feedback: $ra is a register; jr uses its contents, not a label.

steps.title: Mini challenge
steps.prompt: Match each item with its role.
steps.why: These four items cover a complete call.

steps.title: The stack

items: The stack is a region of memory addressed by **$sp** (stack pointer)
It **grows downward**: to push, subtract from $sp, then store
To pop, load, then add back to $sp
Registers must be restored so the caller never notices

blocks.code:
addi $sp, $sp, -4   # make room
sw   $s0, 0($sp)    # save $s0
...                 # procedure uses $s0
lw   $s0, 0($sp)    # restore $s0
addi $sp, $sp, 4    # free the room
jr   $ra

steps.why: A procedure may use $s registers only if it puts the caller’s values back before returning.
steps.real: Every function call in a running program pushes a stack frame like this.

mistake.wrong: The stack grows upward in memory.
mistake.right: In MIPS it grows downward, toward lower addresses.

explainAgain.beginner: A stack of plates: you add and remove at the top, and each caller’s plates stay underneath.

steps.title: Save and restore $s0

blocks.title: Preserving $s0 on the stack
blocks.program:
addi $s0, $zero, 99
addi $a0, $zero, 5
jal usess
j end
usess: addi $sp, $sp, -4
sw $s0, 0($sp)
add $s0, $a0, $a0
add $v0, $s0, $zero
lw $s0, 0($sp)
addi $sp, $sp, 4
jr $ra
end:
blocks.hint: $s0 starts as 99, is reused inside the procedure, and is 99 again at the end.

steps.why: The value 99 is stored at 0x7FFEFFFC while the procedure uses $s0 for something else.

steps.question: What does `$s0` hold after the procedure returns?

reveal.text: The procedure saved 99, used $s0 as a scratch register (10), then restored it. The caller sees **99** again.

steps.result: The result 10 is returned in $v0, not in $s0.

steps.title: Nested calls: save $ra

right.title: With saving $ra
items: The stack keeps each return address

steps.why: A procedure that calls another one must save $ra, because the inner jal overwrites it.

deeper.text: Recursion works the same way: each active call has its own return address and arguments on the stack.

steps.title: A bug: forgetting to save $ra

blocks.title: Nested call without saving $ra
blocks.program:
addi $a0, $zero, 3
jal outer
j end
outer: addi $sp, $sp, -4
addi $a0, $a0, 1
jal inner
addi $sp, $sp, 4
jr $ra
inner: sll $v0, $a0, 2
jr $ra
end:
blocks.hint: The program never finishes; the simulator stops it after 10,000 steps.

steps.why: Compare it with the version that saves $ra; the outer return goes to the wrong place.

steps.title: The correct nested call

blocks.title: Nested calls with $ra saved
blocks.program:
addi $a0, $zero, 3
jal outer
j end
outer: addi $sp, $sp, -4
sw $ra, 0($sp)
addi $a0, $a0, 1
jal inner
lw $ra, 0($sp)
addi $sp, $sp, 4
jr $ra
inner: sll $v0, $a0, 2
jr $ra
end:
blocks.hint: The return address of outer is stored on the stack at 0x7FFEFFFC.

steps.why: The stack holds the return address while the inner call overwrites $ra.

steps.title: Register spilling

blocks.text: A program can have more live values than the 32 registers. The compiler **spills** some values to the stack, loading them back when needed.

steps.why: Spilling is the cost of running out of registers, which is why register allocation matters to compiler writers.
steps.real: Optimizing compilers try hard to keep hot loop values in registers.

steps.title: Spill and reload

blocks.title: Spill $t2, reuse it, then reload
blocks.program:
addi $t0, $zero, 5
addi $t1, $zero, 7
add $t2, $t0, $t1
addi $sp, $sp, -4
sw $t2, 0($sp)
addi $t0, $zero, 2
addi $t1, $zero, 3
add $t2, $t0, $t1
lw $t3, 0($sp)
addi $sp, $sp, 4
sub $t4, $t3, $t2
blocks.hint: (5 + 7) is spilled, (2 + 3) is computed in the same register, then subtracted.

steps.why: 12 is saved on the stack, $t2 is reused for 5, and the reload gives 12 − 5 = 7.

steps.question: Which sequence pushes `$t2` onto the stack?
steps.why: Make room first (stack grows down), then store.
feedback: Storing before moving $sp writes into the previous frame.
Adding 4 moves $sp up, which pops instead of pushing.

steps.title: Think, pair, share
steps.prompt: Why is the return address saved on the stack instead of in a fixed memory location?
steps.answer: A fixed location would be overwritten by the next call, so recursion and nested calls would lose their return addresses. The stack gives each active call its own space, and it is freed automatically when the call returns.

steps.title: Discussion
steps.question: Where do the arguments, local variables and return address of a call live: registers or memory?
ideas: Registers are fastest, but there are few of them.
Memory (the stack) is unlimited but slower.
Calling conventions split the work: a few arguments in registers, the rest on the stack.
A convention lets code from different programmers work together.

steps.question: Which register holds the return address after `jal`?
Translate `if (i == j) f = g + h;` with f,g,h,i,j in $s0 to $s4.
steps.solution: Test the opposite (not equal) and skip the add. Registers: f=$s0, g=$s1, h=$s2, i=$s3, j=$s4.
steps.hint: Which branch instruction tests not equal?
steps.mistake: Using beq and skipping when the values are equal.

steps.question: In the array-sum program, how many times does `lw` execute and what is `$t3`?
steps.solution: The loop body runs for i = 0 to 4, loading 4, 8, 15, 16 and 23; their sum is 66.
steps.hint: The test fails when i reaches 5.

steps.question: In the nested call with $ra saved, where is the return address of `outer` stored and what value is it?
steps.solution: $sp starts at 0x7FFF0000. addi $sp,$sp,-4 gives 0x7FFEFFFC. The jal outer was at 0x00400004, so $ra = 0x00400008.
steps.hint: Subtract 4 from $sp, then use the address of the jal.

steps.question: Trace the for loop `for (i = 0; i < 6; i++) sum += i;` and give the final $t0 (i) and $t1 (sum).
steps.solution: The body runs for i = 0 to 5: 0+1+2+3+4+5 = 15. The test fails when i = 6, so i ends at 6.
steps.title: Exam practice: code tracing

steps.question: Translate `if (a < b) x = y; else x = z;` using a=$s0, b=$s1, x=$s2, y=$s3, z=$s4.
steps.answer: slt $t0,$s0,$s1; beq $t0,$zero,else; add $s2,$zero,$s3; j done; else: add $s2,$zero,$s4; done:
steps.solution: Set the flag with slt, skip to else when it is 0, run the then-part, jump over the else-part.
steps.title: Exam practice: translation

steps.question: A procedure pushes two words onto the stack. $sp was 0x7FFF0000. What is $sp after the pushes, and after the matching pops?
steps.answer: After the pushes 0x7FFEFFF8; after the pops 0x7FFF0000.
steps.solution: Two words = 8 bytes. 0x7FFF0000 − 8 = 0x7FFEFFF8. The pops add 8 back.
steps.title: Exam practice: numerical

steps.question: Explain why a procedure that calls another procedure must save $ra, and a procedure that does not call others (a leaf) need not.
steps.answer: jal overwrites $ra with the new return address, so a nested call would lose the way back to its own caller unless $ra is saved on the stack and restored before jr $ra. A leaf makes no jal, so $ra is never changed and jr $ra works directly.
steps.solution: A strong answer names the overwrite by jal and the stack as the safe place.
steps.mistake: Saying $ra is saved because it is a saved register ($s).
steps.title: Exam practice: conceptual
What you should remember
remember: if and if-else: slt and beq/bne skip the code that should not run.
A loop is a test at the top and a backward jump at the bottom.
a[i] is at base + 4 × i (sll by 2, then add).
jal saves PC + 4 in $ra; jr $ra returns.
Arguments go in $a0-$a3 and results in $v0-$v1.
The stack grows downward: subtract from $sp to push.
Nested procedures must save $ra; extra values are spilled to the stack.

mistakes.right: Use slt then bne or beq.

mistakes.wrong: Element i of an int array is at base + i.
jr $ra is a special return instruction.
mistakes.right: It is an ordinary jump to a register.

steps.title: One-minute summary
steps.summary: Decisions become slt plus beq or bne, loops are tests with backward jumps, and arrays use base + 4i addressing. Procedures use jal to save PC + 4 in $ra and jr to return. Nested calls and extra values use the stack, which grows downward from $sp.

questions.question: Which instruction jumps to a label and saves the return address?
questions.why: jal stores PC + 4 in $ra and jumps.
questions.misconception: j does not save a return address.

questions.statement: The MIPS stack grows toward lower addresses.
questions.misconception: Subtracting 4 makes room for one word.

questions.question: What ends a while loop?
options: A conditional branch whose test fails
questions.why: The test branches out when the condition is false.
questions.misconception: The backward jump alone would repeat forever.

questions.question: Where is a[3] if the int array starts at 0x10010000?
In `if (a == b) c++;` which branch skips the increment?
questions.why: Skip when the values are not equal.
questions.misconception: The branch tests the opposite condition.

questions.question: jal is at 0x00400010. What is $ra afterwards?
$sp is 0x7FFF0000. What is it after pushing three words?
Why does a nested procedure save $ra?
questions.why: jal replaces $ra, which would lose the outer return address.
questions.misconception: Only a procedure that calls others must save $ra.

questions.question: How many times does the body of `for (i = 0; i < 6; i++)` run, and what is i afterwards?
questions.why: i takes the values 0 to 5 (6 iterations); the test fails at i = 6.
questions.misconception: The final value is the one that failed the test.

items.q: How is `if (a < b)` tested in MIPS?
items.a: slt to make a 0/1 flag, then beq or bne.
Saves PC + 4 in $ra and jumps to the label.

items.q: Which direction does the stack grow?

items.a: Storing live values on the stack because registers ran out.
